myth: A fund with a ₹10 NAV is cheaper than one at ₹500.
fact: NAV is just the price of one unit. ₹1 lakh grows by the same % in both if the portfolios perform the same.
A SIP spreads your buying price; it doesn't remove market risk. Over short periods SIP returns can be negative.
send: someone who just started a SIP

myth: You need a lot of money to start investing.
fact: Most mutual funds accept SIPs of ₹100 to ₹500 a month. Starting early matters far more than starting big.

myth: Last year's best fund will be next year's best.
fact: Leadership rotates. Chart-toppers often cool off. Judge funds on consistency across many years and market cycles.
send: someone who picks funds from a 1-year ranking

fact: Five large cap funds own mostly the same stocks. Diversify across categories, not by adding more of the same.

myth: Stop your SIP when markets fall and restart later.
fact: Falls are when a SIP buys the most units. Stopping then gives up the cheapest purchases.
Debt funds carry interest-rate risk and credit risk. They are usually steadier than equity, but not guaranteed.
A payout comes out of your own NAV, which drops by the same amount. For long-term goals, Growth lets compounding work fully.

myth: Index funds are only for beginners.
fact: Many professionals use index funds as a low-cost core. Beating the index consistently is hard, even for experts.
send: someone who looks down on index funds

myth: Small caps always give the highest returns.
fact: Small caps can lead for years and then fall 50%+ and stay down for a long time. They need a 7+ year horizon.
send: someone going all-in on small caps

myth: Timing the market is the key to wealth.
fact: Missing a handful of the best days can sharply cut long-term returns, and those days often come right after the worst ones.

myth: Momentum investing is just gambling on hot stocks.
fact: Systematic momentum is rule-based: rank, buy strength, exit weakness, rebalance on schedule. It is among the most researched factors in finance.
send: a friend who trades on tips

myth: High returns mean a good fund.
fact: Returns without context mislead. Compare with the benchmark and look at how much the fund fell in bad years.

myth: Once invested, you never need to review.
fact: Review once a year: check allocation, overlap and whether each fund still does its job. Then leave it alone.
send: someone who hasn't checked in years
